Bought subscribers: the mistake that keeps costing
Growth · September 26, 2026 · 4 min read · Fast Scheduler team
Channels rarely die from one big mistake. They bleed from small ones that never announce themselves. Fifteen of them, each with the fix — collected from watching hundreds of channels stall.
1. Stacking posts.
Five posts in ten minutes = one muted channel. Space them hours apart — schedule the spacing, not just the sending.
2. Dead-hour publishing.
Posting at 3 AM because that’s when you finished writing. Schedule for the audience’s prime time, not your free time.
3. Caption walls.
1,000-character captions on photos get truncated in previews. Hook in 60 characters, details in a text post.
4. No signature.
Forwards without the channel name are free advertising you never receive. Toggle “sign messages” on.
5. The midnight queue dump.
Batch-writing is good; releasing it all at once isn’t. Any scheduler (ControllerBot,
, ManyBot) fixes this permanently.
6. Topic drift.
Subscribers came for a promise. Every off-topic post mutes a few of them.
7. The feed dump.
Unfiltered RSS/news reposts make you replaceable. Curation is the product.
8. “Part 2” bait.
Splitting value across posts to inflate views teaches readers not to open part 1.
9. Never asking.
No polls, no questions, no comment replies — a channel without interaction signals decays in the recommendation surfaces.
10. Buying subscribers.
Bot followers never read, and TGStat displays the damage permanently — swaps and advertisers check it before you get a reply.
11. Swapping with zombies.
A 10K channel with a 8% view ratio delivers nothing. Vet on TGStat/Telemetr first.
12. Ignoring the ratio.
Views ÷ subscribers is your currency everywhere; not knowing your number is sailing blind.
13. Growing before retaining.
Buying ads into a leaky channel. Retention data first, ads second.
14. Manual-everything.
Posting by hand daily collapses around week six. Batch + schedule is the fix — this is the mistake behind most dead channels.
15. No backup.
A channel’s asset is its content pipeline. Export it periodically (every major scheduler has an export) — “it won’t happen to me” is not a plan.
None of these fixes cost money. That’s the point: Telegram punishes sloppiness, not poverty.
Every mistake on this list is detectable early by the same ritual. Quarterly, sit with the channel for five minutes and answer five questions.
1) Ratio:
count the last 20 posts — value vs self-serving — is it past 70/30?
2) Rhythm:
look at the timestamps — are there dead hours, multi-post bursts, weeks the channel went dark?
3) ERR trend:
views ÷ subscribers on the last ten posts — up, flat, or sliding?
4) The pinned post:
open the channel as a stranger would — does the pin still tell a newcomer what this is and why to stay?
5) The admin list:

any bot or human with rights nobody remembers granting? Five answers, five lines in a note, and the two or three fixes that fall out go into next month's calendar. Channels don't die from the mistake nobody warned them about — they die from the six they noticed and postponed.

It deserves its own section because it's the only mistake that compounds. Purchased subscribers — the thousand-for-$10 accounts — do four things at once: they crater your ERR (every future ERR-based decision — ad pricing, swap attractiveness, directory ranking — now reads worse than reality), they poison Similar Channels (the graph links you to the other channels those bots pollute), they make every future analytics decision wrong (you're optimizing for an audience that doesn't exist), and they're nearly irreversible — Telegram doesn't offer bulk removal of bots and fakes, so a polluted channel either culls by hand or lives with the number. The honest growth arithmetic: 500 real subscribers with a 45% ERR out-earn 5,000 purchased ones with a 4% ERR in every commercial conversation, every swap, every month. There is no version of this purchase that pays for itself.
Common questions
What is the most common Telegram channel mistake?
Inconsistent publishing — usually manual posting that collapses under real life. It compounds into every other metric: view ratios, recommendation eligibility, swap credibility.
Are bought Telegram subscribers really that bad?
Yes — they never view posts, so they permanently depress your view-to-subscriber ratio, which TGStat displays publicly. Swap partners and advertisers see it before you can explain it.
How do I know if my channel is dying?
Falling first-hour views with stable subscriber count, rising mute indicators (fewer poll votes), and churn after every post burst. All three are visible in your scheduler’s per-post stats.
How often should I back up my channel content?
Monthly, and before any big change. Scheduler exports capture scheduled and recurring posts — rebuilding months of queue from memory is worse.
